theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: For manual handling at work, what should an employer try to do first?
options: Avoid the handling where it can be avoided
Train every worker to lift any load they are given
Give each worker a back support belt
Set one weight limit for every worker

questions.stem: What is a worker's main duty about manual handling at work?
options: Lift whatever the supervisor asks, at any weight
Buy their own lifting gear for each job
Follow the safe system and use the aids given
Decide alone to skip the risk assessment

questions.stem: A manual handling risk assessment looks at four things, often remembered as TILE. What do the letters stand for?
options: Time, Injury, Lift, Equipment
Task, Individual, Load, Environment
Tools, Instructions, Load, Effort
Task, Instructions, Lifting, Equipment

questions.stem: Which of these tasks carries the highest risk of back injury?
options: Lifting a light box from a bench to a trolley
Carrying a load close to the waist on level ground
Pushing a well-kept trolley on a smooth floor
Twisting while holding a load at arm's length

questions.stem: Why is a load held at arm's length much harder on the back than the same load held close to the body?
options: The load really gets heavier as it moves further out
The arms take all the weight when straight
The strain on the back grows with the distance
The legs cannot bend while the arms are out

questions.stem: A team member is back at work after a back injury. What should the team leader do before giving him lifting work?
options: Review his tasks and get advice on what is safe
Give him the heaviest jobs to build his strength
Tell him to wear a back belt and carry on
Let him decide alone, with no change to the plan

questions.stem: Steel must be carried across an open yard in Old Harbour in the midday heat. Which control is most suitable?
options: Work faster to finish before the worst heat
Take gloves off so hands can grip better
Skip the rest breaks so the job ends sooner
Plan shaded breaks, give water and share the work

questions.stem: The route from the store to the welding bay has a step and an oily patch. What should be done before steel is moved along it?
options: Move the steel quickly so nobody stays on the oil
Clean the oil and plan a way round the step
Put a sign at the step and carry on as normal
Carry the steel higher so feet can be seen

questions.stem: Which of these loads is hardest to handle safely, even though it is not heavy?
options: A large, thin sheet that catches the wind
A small, compact box with good handles on each side
A short bar that is easy to grip
A bag of rods placed on a trolley

questions.stem: Which aid is best for moving a pallet of electrode boxes about 30 m across a smooth, level floor?
options: Two people carrying it by hand
Rollers placed under the pallet
A pallet truck
A chain block hung from a beam

questions.stem: A 400 kg welded frame must be lifted onto stands in the workshop. Which method is best?
options: Six trainees lifting it together by hand, all at once
A rated chain block on a frame, with rated slings
A car jack under one corner at a time
A forklift driven by any willing trainee

questions.stem: What does the SWL (safe working load) marked on a chain block tell you?
options: The weight of the chain block itself
The least weight it is able to lift
The height it can lift a load to
The most it may lift in normal use

questions.stem: A permanent lifting magnet is used to move steel plate. Which condition makes the lift unsafe?
options: A clean, flat plate within the magnet's rating
The magnet switched on fully before the plate is lifted
A thin, curved or painted plate that cuts the grip
The plate raised only a little at first

questions.stem: Why must a plate clamp never be used to lift two plates at once?
options: The lower plate is not gripped and can slide out
Two plates are always too heavy for any clamp
The clamp's lock only works on stainless steel
Two plates make the clamp's jaws grip much too tight

questions.stem: Which is the main safety rule for using a forklift to move steel at the Centre?
options: Anyone may drive it if they go slowly
People may ride on the forks to steady a load
Loads may be carried high for a better view
Only a trained, authorised driver may drive it

questions.stem: When you are about to lift a heavy box from the floor, which step comes first?
options: Grip it with the fingertips and pull it up as fast as you can
Check the load and route, and decide if help is needed
Bend the back and keep the legs straight
Lift it in one quick jerk to save effort

questions.stem: Why are the feet placed apart, with one foot a little forward, when lifting?
options: To give a steady base and keep balance
So the back can twist more easily
So the arms can take all of the weight
So the knees can stay locked straight

questions.stem: While holding a load, a welder must put it on a bench to his side. What should he do?
options: Twist from the waist and keep his feet still
Throw the load the last short distance
Turn by moving his feet, not by twisting
Lean sideways and stretch out his arms

questions.stem: A loaded trolley must be moved. Is it usually better to push or to pull it, and why?
options: Pull, as you can walk backwards safely
Push, as you use body weight and can see ahead
Pull, as the arms then take all the load
Either, as there is no difference at all

questions.stem: Three trainees will carry a 6 m length of steel pipe. Which is the safest way?
options: Each one lifts when ready and walks at own pace
The strongest person takes one end alone
Drag it along the floor to save effort
One leader calls the moves and all act together

questions.stem: Why can two people not safely lift twice what one person can lift?
options: Two people always get in each other's way
The load gets heavier when two people hold it
They seldom share the weight or move exactly together
Only one of them is allowed to bend the knees in a lift

questions.stem: When choosing people for a team lift, which is good practice?
options: People of similar height and build, briefed on the lift
The tallest and the shortest people, so that they balance
Whoever is free, with no briefing needed
As many people as can reach the load

questions.stem: A steel plate is 1.5 m × 1 m × 6 mm. Steel weighs about 7 850 kg per cubic metre. About how heavy is the plate?
options: About 7 kg
About 47 kg
About 118 kg
About 71 kg

questions.stem: A 6 m length of steel angle has a mass of 4.5 kg per metre. What is its total mass?
options: 27 kg
24 kg
45 kg

questions.stem: A bundle holds 8 lengths of flat bar at 18 kg each, on a 20 kg pallet. What total load must the lifting gear take?
options: 164 kg
144 kg
180 kg
162 kg

questions.stem: Two equal sling legs lift a load. As the angle between the legs gets wider, what happens to the force in each leg?
options: It gets smaller
It stays at half the load
It gets larger
It drops to nothing

questions.stem: A two-leg sling is rated for angles of up to 90° between the legs. Rigged on a wide frame, the legs would be at about 120°. What should you do?
options: Use it, as the rating is the same at any angle
Use longer legs so the angle is 90° or less
Use it, but lift the load more quickly
Tie a knot in one leg to even out the angle

questions.stem: Two trained workers can each lift 25 kg safely alone. A common guide says a team of two can handle about two-thirds of their total. Can they carry a 60 kg load?
options: Yes: together they can lift 50 kg, near enough
Yes: two careful people can lift any load
No: two people should never lift together
No: the guide gives about 33 kg, so use an aid

questions.stem: Before a welded frame is lifted with a chain block, where should the hook be?
options: Above the heaviest end of the frame
Off to one side so the load swings clear
Right above the load's centre of gravity
Above the corner nearest the operator

questions.stem: A load tilts as soon as it leaves the floor. What should be done?
options: Lower it, adjust the hook or slings, and try again
Carry on and push it level by hand in the air
Lift it higher so it can settle by itself
Have someone stand on the low side as weight

questions.stem: Why is a load first lifted just a few centimetres and held there?
options: To let the chain warm up before the lift
To give the team time for a short break
To measure how high the stands need to be
To check the balance, slings and brake

questions.stem: A flat webbing sling has a cut in its edge and its label is missing. What should be done?
options: Use it for light loads only from now on, and mark it
Take it out of use and destroy or quarantine it
Tape over the cut and keep using it
Write a new rating on it with a marker

questions.stem: Which fault means a wire rope sling must be taken out of use?
options: Broken wires, kinks or a crushed part
A light coat of rope grease
A clear rating tag on the eye
Some dust and dry dirt on the outside of the rope

questions.stem: When a screw-pin shackle is fitted to a lifting point, what must be done with the pin?
options: Leave it two turns loose so it can move
Swap it for any bolt that fits the holes
Screw it fully home so it seats properly
Leave it out when the load is light

questions.stem: Why should a lifting hook have a safety catch (latch) that works?
options: To let the hook lift a heavier load
To stop the sling slipping off the hook
To lock the chain block's brake on
To show that the hook was inspected

questions.stem: A sling must pass round the sharp edge of a steel beam. What should be done?
options: Pull the sling tight so it cannot slide
Use a thinner sling that bends more easily
Wet the sling so the edge cuts less
Fit packing or edge guards at the edge

questions.stem: Why must nobody stand or walk under a load hanging from a chain block?
options: They would block the operator's view of the hook
The load may sway and mark their clothes
The gear could fail or the load slip and fall
Shade from the load makes it hard to see

questions.stem: A frame is being lowered onto stands. Where should the people guiding it keep their hands and feet?
options: Clear of any gap between the load and the stands
Under the load, ready to take some of the weight
On top of the stands, to line the frame up
Right under the hook, to steady the chain

questions.stem: Lifting gear is given a thorough examination by a competent person at set times. What else should happen?
options: Nothing, until the next set examination
Gear is used until it fails, then replaced
Only new gear is ever looked at
The user checks it by eye before each use

questions.stem: Large thin steel sheets (2.4 m × 1.2 m) must be carried to the guillotine. Which method is safest?
options: One person dragging each sheet flat on the floor
Two people in cut-resistant gloves, sheet on edge
Two people with bare hands for a better grip
Carried flat overhead to clear the benches

questions.stem: What is a musculoskeletal disorder (MSD)?
options: Pain or injury in muscles, joints or the back
An illness caught from breathing in welding fumes
A burn from hot metal or sparks
A loss of hearing from loud noise

questions.stem: A trainee says his lower back has ached for a week since he started carrying steel. What should the team leader do?
options: Say it is normal for new workers and tell him to keep going
Give him heavier steel to toughen him up
Record it, change his tasks, and send him for advice
Wait and act only if he can no longer work

questions.stem: A chain block slips and the load drops about 100 mm, but nobody is hurt. What should happen?
options: Carry on, as nobody was hurt
Stop using it, tag it out and report it
Tighten the chain by hand and carry on
Use it for lighter loads from now on

questions.stem: You see a trainee lifting a box with a bent back and straight legs. What is the best action?
options: Shout at him from across the workshop to stop
Leave it, as he has not been hurt yet
Write him up but say nothing to him
Stop him, show the right way, watch him try

questions.stem: Before a group moves a 300 kg fabrication out to a truck, what should the team leader prepare?
options: A purchase order for new slings
An invoice for the customer
A simple lift plan: weight, gear and roles
A timesheet for the truck driver and the helpers

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

essays.stem: Explain how you would carry out and record a manual handling risk assessment for carrying 6 m lengths of steel pipe from the yard to the cutting bench, using the TILE headings.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first watch the job being done and talk to the people who do it. Under Task, I would note the distance, whether people must twist, stoop or carry the pipe at arm's length, how often it is done and whether there are rest breaks. Under Individual, I would note who does the work, their training, health and any past injury, and whether the job needs unusual strength. Under Load, I would work out the weight of each length from the mass per metre, and note that it is long, awkward, may be hot from the sun, oily or sharp at the ends. Under Environment, I would look at the route: the floor, steps, doors, corners, space to turn, light, heat and rain. For each risk I would decide a control, such as a pipe trolley or rack on wheels, a team carry with a leader, gloves, a clear route and shade breaks. I would write it on the risk assessment form with the date and my name, tell the team, and review it if anything changes or someone is hurt.
markingPoints: Task: distance, posture, twisting, how often
Individual: training, health, past injury, strength needed
Load: weight worked out, length, grip, heat, sharp or oily ends
Environment: route, floor, steps, space, light, heat and weather
Controls chosen, recorded with date and name, shared with team and reviewed

essays.stem: Explain the order in which manual handling risks should be controlled (avoid, assess, reduce), and give a fabrication shop example of each.
essays.modelAnswer: The first step is to avoid manual handling where it can be avoided. For example, steel can be delivered by the supplier's truck crane straight onto the rack beside the saw, or parts can be cut and welded where they will be used, so they do not need to be carried. Where handling cannot be avoided, the next step is to assess the risk properly, looking at the task, the individual, the load and the environment, and writing it down. For example, before trainees carry gates to the paint area, the team leader checks the weight, the route and who will do it. The third step is to reduce the risk as low as is reasonably possible. This can be done with handling aids such as trolleys, pallet trucks, chain blocks and plate clamps; by making loads smaller, such as ordering shorter lengths or splitting a bundle; by team lifting with a leader; by improving the route; and by training people in safe lifting. Finally, the controls are checked and reviewed.
markingPoints: Avoid first, with a workshop example
Assess next (task, individual, load, environment), with an example
Reduce: handling aids, with examples
Reduce: smaller loads, team lifts, better routes, training
Check and review the controls

essays.stem: Describe the steps of a safe lift of a 15 kg box of steel parts from the floor onto a bench, and explain how you would teach and check this with a new trainee.
essays.modelAnswer: Before lifting, check the box: its weight, whether it is stable, and whether the sides are sharp or oily. Check the route and clear a place on the bench. Stand close to the box with the feet apart, one foot slightly forward. Bend the knees and hips, keep the back in its natural curve and get a firm grip, with gloves if needed. Keep the box close to the body and the heaviest side nearest you. Lift smoothly by straightening the legs, keeping the head up and not jerking. Do not twist; turn by moving the feet. Put the box down by bending the knees, then slide it into place on the bench. To teach a new trainee, I would explain why each step matters, then show the lift myself. Next the trainee would try it while I watch, and I would correct any fault straight away, such as a bent back or twisting. I would have him repeat it until it is right, check again later on real jobs, and record the training.
markingPoints: Checks the load and the route before lifting
Feet apart, knees bent, back in its natural curve, firm grip, load close
Smooth lift using the legs, no twisting, turns with the feet, safe set-down
Teaching: explain, show, trainee tries, correct faults
Checks again later on the job and records the training

essays.stem: Explain how you would plan and lead a team carry of a long, awkward load, such as a 4 m welded gate, from the workshop to a truck.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would work out the weight of the gate and decide whether a team carry is safe at all, or whether a trolley, gantry or forklift is needed. If a team carry is right, I would choose enough people of similar height and strength, all trained in lifting, and make sure they wear gloves and safety boots. I would walk the route first, clearing it and checking doors, corners, steps and the truck bed height. I would brief the team: where each person holds the gate, the route, and the words we will use, such as 'ready, lift', 'walk', 'stop' and 'lower'. One person, usually me, gives all the commands. We lift together on the command, keep the gate close and level, walk in step, and stop at corners to plan the turn. At the truck we set it down on packing first if needed, then lift it onto the bed together. Afterwards I would ask the team how it went and note any changes for next time.
markingPoints: Works out the weight and considers aids before a team carry
Chooses suitable, trained people with PPE
Checks and clears the route and the truck height
Briefs roles and agreed commands; one person gives the commands
Lifts, moves and lowers together, then reviews

essays.stem: A small fabrication shop in Montego Bay must move steel plate, long bars, gas cylinders and finished gates every day. Compare suitable handling aids and say which you would choose for each, and why.
essays.modelAnswer: For steel plate, I would use a plate clamp or lifting magnet on a chain block hung from a gantry, so nobody has to lift heavy plates by hand, and a plate trolley to move them. A plate clamp suits single plates and is simple; a magnet is quick but must be rated for the plate and used only on flat, clean plate. For long bars and pipe, I would use a long trolley or a pair of bar dollies and store the bars on a rack at waist height, which avoids bending to the floor. For gas cylinders, I would use a proper cylinder trolley with a chain, so they stay upright and are never rolled by the valve or carried. For finished gates, I would use a gantry or an engine-type crane for loading, or a team carry with a leader for lighter gates, with packing and a flat trolley over longer distances. In each case I would check the aid's rating against the load, train the staff to use it, and keep it inspected and in good repair.
markingPoints: Plate: clamp or magnet on a chain block or gantry, with a reason
Bars and pipe: long trolley or dollies and waist-height racks, with a reason
Cylinders: cylinder trolley, chained upright
Gates: lifting aid or planned team carry, with a reason
Checks rating against the load, trains users and keeps aids inspected

essays.stem: Describe how to check chain slings, wire rope slings, webbing slings, shackles and hooks before use, and what you must do with any gear that is faulty.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would check that every item has a legible rating tag or mark and an identity number, and that it is in date for its thorough examination. On a chain sling I would look for stretched, bent, twisted, nicked or worn links, and check the hooks and the master link. On a wire rope sling I would look for broken wires, kinks, crushing, birdcaging, rust and damaged eyes or ferrules. On a webbing or round sling I would look for cuts, tears, burns, chemical damage, worn stitching and a missing label. On a shackle I would check that the body is not bent or worn and that the pin is the right one and screws fully home. On a hook I would check that it has not opened out or twisted, and that the safety latch works. Any faulty item, or any item with no tag, must be taken out of use at once, tagged 'Do not use', and put in a locked or marked quarantine area. I would report it in writing so it is repaired by a competent person or destroyed, and record it on the gear register.
markingPoints: Checks rating mark, identity and in-date examination on every item
Chain and wire rope faults named
Webbing faults, shackle and hook checks named
Faulty or untagged gear taken out of use, tagged and quarantined
Reported, repaired or destroyed by a competent person, and recorded

essays.stem: Explain why the load in each leg of a two-leg sling rises as the angle between the legs gets wider. Then explain how you would work out the weight of a welded frame and choose a sling for it.
essays.modelAnswer: When the two legs hang straight down, each leg carries half the load. As the legs spread out, each leg pulls partly sideways as well as up. Only the upward part of the pull holds the load, so the total pull in each leg must grow to keep holding the same weight. At an angle of 120° between the legs, each leg carries as much as the whole load. This is why slings are rated for a range of angles, usually up to 90°, and why very wide angles must be avoided. To find the weight of a frame, I would list each piece from the drawing, find its length and its mass per metre from the steel tables, or work out plate volumes and use about 7 850 kg per cubic metre, then add them up and add a little for welds and fittings. I would then choose a sling whose rating at the angle I will use is more than the weight, with legs long enough to keep the angle at 90° or less, and check it before use.
markingPoints: Straight legs share the load equally (half each)
Wider legs pull sideways too, so the force in each leg grows
Very wide angles are dangerous; slings are rated for an angle range
Works out the frame weight from lengths and mass per metre or volume and density
Chooses a sling rated above the weight at the angle used, with long enough legs

essays.stem: Explain the main causes and early signs of back and other musculoskeletal injuries in fabrication work, and how a team leader can prevent them over a working week.
essays.modelAnswer: Musculoskeletal injuries affect the back, neck, shoulders, arms, wrists and knees. In fabrication they are caused by lifting heavy or awkward steel, twisting and stooping, holding a load away from the body, repeating the same movement for hours (such as grinding or hammering), working in cramped positions under a job, and tiredness. Early signs include aches or stiffness that last after work, pain when bending, tingling or numbness in the hands, weakness and poor sleep because of pain. To prevent them, a team leader can plan the work so that handling aids are used, steel is stored at waist height and jobs are set on stands at a good working height. The leader can rotate tasks so nobody grinds or lifts all day, plan short breaks and water in the heat, and make sure everyone is trained in safe lifting. The leader should watch how people work, correct poor technique and encourage people to report pain early, so tasks can be changed before a small strain becomes a serious injury.
markingPoints: Names the body parts affected
Causes: heavy or awkward loads, twisting, repetition, poor posture, tiredness
Early signs: lasting aches, stiffness, tingling, numbness, weakness
Prevention: aids, good working heights and storage, task rotation and breaks
Training, supervision and early reporting of pain

essays.stem: A trainee strains his back while lifting a gate. Explain how you would deal with it: the care of the trainee, the report, finding the cause and the actions to stop it happening again.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would stop the work, make the area safe and see to the trainee. I would not move him if he could not move by himself, would call the first aider, and would get medical help if the pain was severe or he had numbness or weakness. If he could walk, he would rest and be sent to a doctor or clinic for a check. Then I would fill in the accident report the same day: his name, the date, time and place, what he was doing, what happened, the injury and the first aid given, and the names of any witnesses. Next I would find out why it happened. I would look at the gate's weight, how it was lifted, how many people helped, whether an aid was available, the route and whether he had been trained. From this I would decide on actions, such as using a gantry or trolley for gates, a planned team carry with a leader, training, or a better route. I would brief the team, update the risk assessment and check that the actions were carried out.
markingPoints: Makes the area safe, gives first aid and gets medical help when needed
Writes a full accident report with the key details and witnesses
Investigates the cause: load, method, people, aids, route, training
Decides and records actions to prevent it happening again
Briefs the team, updates the risk assessment and follows up

essays.stem: Explain how the work area and conditions affect manual handling risk on a Jamaican building site, such as heat, rain, rough ground, slopes, space and light. Say how you would control each.
essays.modelAnswer: Heat and strong sun make people tired and sweaty, so their grip is poor, and steel left in the sun can burn the hands. I would plan heavy handling for the cooler morning, give water and shaded breaks, and use gloves. Rain makes steel, mud and boots slippery and can wash out the ground. I would stop handling in heavy rain, wipe or dry loads, and lay boards or gravel on the route. Rough or soft ground and slopes make people trip or lose balance, and make trolleys hard to push. I would choose and clear a firm, level route, use boards or ramps, and use wheeled aids only where the ground suits them. Tight space forces people to twist and stoop, so I would clear room to work, set loads down near where they are needed, and use mechanical lifting where people cannot stand properly. Poor light hides trip hazards, so I would work in daylight or add lighting. Wind can catch sheets and panels, so I would avoid carrying them in strong wind and use extra people or aids.
markingPoints: Heat and sun: tiredness, grip, hot steel, with controls
Rain: slippery surfaces and ground, with controls
Rough ground and slopes: trips and balance, with controls
Space: twisting and stooping, with controls
Light or wind: hidden hazards or sheets catching the wind, with controls

practical1.title: Manual handling risk assessment and a planned move of mixed steel stock with handling aids
practical1.brief: Your group will plan and carry out the safe move of a delivery of mixed steel stock from the delivery area to the store racks, as the assessor sets out. The load will include: at least two 6 m lengths of pipe or angle, several thin steel sheets, a box or pallet of electrode boxes, and a bundle of short flat bar. First, as a group, walk the route and complete a manual handling risk assessment using the TILE headings (task, individual, load, environment). Work out the weight of each item from the mass per metre or the plate size, and write it on the plan. For each item, choose the method (pallet truck, trolley, sheet clamps, team carry or a lifting aid) and say why. Each member takes a turn as team leader for one item: briefs the team, gives the commands and checks the others' technique. Every member takes part in each move. Stack the stock safely on the racks, with sheets on edge or flat as the Centre's racks allow, and long lengths secured. Finish with a short report: what went well, any problems, and one change you would make. Photograph each stage below. Hand in the risk assessment, the weight calculations, the move plan, the report and the photos once for the whole group.
materials: Mixed steel stock set out by the assessor (6 m lengths of pipe or angle, thin sheets, flat bar, a box or pallet of electrode boxes)
Pallet truck, flat trolley or bar dollies, and sheet lifting clamps if the Centre has them
Cut-resistant gloves, safety boots and hard hats for every member
Steel tables (mass per metre) or the assessor's weight data, a tape measure and a calculator
Manual handling risk assessment form, move plan form and report sheet
Barrier tape or cones to close off the route while moving
photos: The route walked and checked, with any hazards marked
The completed risk assessment and weight calculations
The team briefing before a team carry
A team carry of a long length, with the leader giving commands
A handling aid in use (pallet truck, trolley or sheet clamp)
The stock stacked and secured on the racks
The completed move plan and report
checklist: Took part in the TILE risk assessment and pointed out at least one hazard
Worked out the weight of at least one item correctly
Chose a suitable method or aid for an item and explained why
As leader, briefed the team clearly and gave clear commands
Used safe lifting technique: load close, knees bent, no twisting
Used the handling aids correctly and within their rating
Stacked stock safely and helped write the report
safety: Wear gloves, safety boots and hard hats; handle sheet edges with care
Do not lift anything you think is too heavy; ask for help or an aid
Close off the route while moving long lengths, and stop at corners and doors
Use aids only within their rating; follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
Drink water and take breaks in the shade in hot weather

practical2.title: Planned lift of a welded frame with a chain block, slings and shackles, with gear checks and a lift record
practical2.brief: Your group will plan and carry out the lift of a small welded steel frame or fabrication (the assessor will choose one well within the rating of the Centre's lifting frame and chain block), raise it, set it on trestles or stands, and lower it back to the floor. First, as a group, work out the frame's weight from its drawing, using the mass per metre of each piece, and mark its centre of gravity. Choose the slings and shackles, and check that their rating at the sling angle you will use is more than the weight. Inspect every item of lifting gear before use (chain block, slings, shackles, hooks and latches) and record the results on the gear check sheet; any faulty item is tagged and set aside. Write a short lift plan: the weight, the gear, the sling angle, the route, the exclusion zone and each person's role. Roles are: lift leader (gives signals), chain block operator, rigger, tag-line holder, and area guard and recorder. The group does the lift at least twice so that every member takes at least two roles, one of them leader or operator. Do a trial lift of a few centimetres first and check the balance and the brake. Photograph each stage below. Hand in the weight calculation, the gear check sheet, the lift plan and the photos once for the whole group.
materials: A small welded steel frame or fabrication, with its drawing
Lifting frame (gantry or A-frame) with a rated chain block
Rated chain or webbing slings and shackles, all tagged and in date
A tag line, edge protectors or packing, and two trestles or stands
Steel tables (mass per metre), tape measure and calculator
Barrier tape or cones for the exclusion zone
Gear check sheet and lift plan form
photos: The weight calculation and the centre of gravity marked on the frame
The lifting gear laid out and being inspected, with the gear check sheet
The frame rigged, with the hook above the centre of gravity
The trial lift a few centimetres off the floor
The frame set down on the trestles, with the exclusion zone in place
The completed lift plan and gear check sheet
checklist: Worked out the frame's weight correctly and helped find its centre of gravity
Inspected lifting gear correctly and recorded the results
Chose slings and shackles rated above the load at the angle used
Rigged the load correctly: shackle pins home, latches closed, edges protected
As leader or operator, carried out the trial lift and gave or followed clear signals
Kept hands and feet clear of pinch points and never stood under the load
Helped complete the lift plan and left the gear clean and stored
safety: Use only tagged, in-date gear within its rating; follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
Keep the exclusion zone closed; nobody stands or walks under the load
Only the lift leader gives signals, but anyone may call 'stop' at any time
Wear hard hats, gloves and safety boots
Lower the load if it tilts or the gear looks wrong, and fix the problem before lifting again
